newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Suspicious Swiss guard gives Jews bank documents.
newsitem.headline: Suspicious Swiss guard gives Jews bank documents.

text.p: A suspicious security guard at Switzerland's biggest bank stole old documents bound for the shredder and turned them over to Swiss Jews in the belief he could help trace Holocaust funds, officials said on Tuesday.

The guard told a news conference called by the Zurich Jewish leaders that he was acting on his conscience when he smuggled out books, papers and documents dating back to 1875, dealing Swiss banks a fresh shock in the row over missing Jewish wealth.
"To me it was clear that these were documents that should not be destroyed," said Christoph Meili, 28.
The documents, initially turned over to the Jewish group, are now in the hands of local police while Zurich prosecutors examine the case.

Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) acknowledged the plan to shred the wartime-era documents was a clear violation of the government's ban on destroying any material that could be important in the search for dormant Jewish accounts.
But it denied the documents were related in any way to dormant accounts. Jewish groups have alleged Swiss banks are still hoarding billions of dollars in Nazi victims' wealth.
"UBS strongly regrets the incident," it said in a statement, noting the employee had also violated the bank's own blanket ban on destroying any documents.
A UBS spokesman said the documents were purely historical in nature and of no relevance to the search for lost Jewish money.
"There were no client documents," she said, adding: "In principle the documents and the Holocaust debate have nothing to do with each other."

But Meili said the documents, which he stuffed in a shopping bag under his shirt and spirited out of UBS headquarters on Bahnhofstrasse, included data on "forced auctions" of properties in Berlin between the years 1930 and 1940.
He also claimed to have saved records of loans granted to both Swiss and German firms between the years 1920 and 1926, along with hand-written minutes of central bank meetings dating back to 1875.
The documents stem from the Eidgenoessische Bank, which UBS acquired in 1945.

A bank spokeswoman said a UBS employee had been searching through the bank's files and released for shredding some of the documents which he considered unimportant. They included minutes of meetings, annual reports and other such documents, she said.

She said the documents were turned over to UBS some time ago and examined by an historian who determined that some were perhaps interesting for UBS from an historical point of view, but that they were not in his opinion otherwise important.

UBS said it was cooperating with prosecutors, but its own investigation showed the employee had no intention of destroying documents that could be of use in the inquiry into Swiss relations with Nazi Germany during World War Two.

The Swiss government last month banned the destruction of any documents that could be used in the probe. It has agreed to lift banking secrecy for dormant accounts and let an international panel of historians conduct a review.
